title: Short Straddle Strategy: Payoff, Breakeven, Risks and Nifty Example
summary: Learn the short straddle strategy with a Nifty example, payoff table, breakeven and risks. Build and backtest your rules on AlgoTest before going live.
body_markdown:
A **short straddle strategy** involves selling a call option and a put option on the same underlying, at the same strike price and with the same expiry. You receive both premiums upfront. The position benefits if the combined cost of buying those options back falls, but a large market move can produce losses far greater than the premium collected.


For a Nifty options trader, understanding the payoff is the starting point. Entry time, expiry selection, exit rules and execution costs determine how a particular trading approach behaves.


This guide explains the mechanics with a numerical example, then shows how to build the position and test a rule-based version on[AlgoTest.](https://algotest.in/?utm_source=blog&utm_medium=internal&utm_campaign=seo&utm_content=main-page&utm_term=algotest&utm_source=blog&utm_medium=internal&utm_campaign=seo&utm_term=algotest&utm_content=main-page)


## What is a short straddle?


A short straddle combines two[option-selling positions](https://algotest.in/blog/what-is-option-selling/) :


Leg


Action


Strike and expiry


Call option, or CE


Sell


Same as the put


Put option, or PE


Sell


Same as the call


Both legs use equal quantities. Traders commonly select the at-the-money, or ATM, strike, which is close to the underlying's current price.


For example, if Nifty is near 25,000, selling a 25,000 CE and a 25,000 PE with the same expiry creates an ATM short straddle.


The premium received is the maximum potential gross profit if the position is held to expiry. It is not a guaranteed return. Margin must support the position, and closing it can cost more than the initial credit.

The call and put have the same expiry. The 65-unit quantity reflects the Nifty market-lot revision in the[NSE circular on index derivatives lot sizes](https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/content/circulars/FAOP70616.pdf) . Always check the selected contract's current lot size before placing an order.


These premiums are illustrative, not live quotes. You can inspect available strikes and premiums on the[AlgoTest Nifty option chain](https://algotest.in/nifty-option-chain) .


### Maximum profit and breakeven


For this position, before transaction costs:


-


**Maximum profit:** total premium × quantity = 250 × 65 = **₹16,250** .


-


**Lower breakeven:** strike − total premium = 25,000 − 250 = **24,750** .


-


**Upper breakeven:** strike + total premium = 25,000 + 250 = **25,250** .


Maximum profit occurs if Nifty's final settlement value is exactly 25,000, so both options expire without intrinsic value. Between the two breakeven levels, the position has a gross profit at expiry. Beyond either level, it has a gross loss.


### Short straddle payoff at expiry

Brokerage, taxes, exchange charges and other applicable costs reduce these results. The theoretical breakeven points therefore produce a net loss after costs; the net profitable range is narrower.


## Why intraday profit differs from the expiry payoff


An expiry payoff table does not tell you the price at which you can close the options earlier.


Suppose you collected 250 points and later buy back both options for a combined 200 points. Your gross profit is:


**(250 − 200) × 65 = ₹3,250**


If the combined buyback price rises to 300 points, your gross loss is:


**(250 − 300) × 65 = −₹3,250**


Before expiry,[option premiums](https://algotest.in/blog/black-scholes-option-pricing-model/) still reflect remaining time and implied volatility. Nifty can remain inside the expiry breakeven range while the open position shows a loss. Always distinguish an expiry payoff from a mark-to-market result.

## How time decay and volatility affect a short straddle


The main sensitivities of an unhedged short straddle are:


Factor


Typical effect, with other factors unchanged


Time decay, or theta


Helps the seller as option time value declines


Rising implied volatility, or vega exposure


Hurts the seller by increasing option values


Falling implied volatility


Helps by reducing option values


Large underlying price movement


Can create losses that outweigh time decay


An ATM short straddle may begin with roughly offsetting directional exposures. That balance changes as the underlying moves. Near expiry, directional exposure can change quickly, which makes “only a little time left” an inadequate reason to sell options.


The[Options Industry Council's short straddle guide](https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/short-straddle) explains these volatility and time-decay characteristics in more detail.


## How to build and backtest a short straddle on AlgoTest


Use Strategy Builder to study a specific position. Use the time-based workflow to[backtest options strategies](https://algotest.in/blog/how-to-backtest-options-trading-strategies-with-examples/) with repeatable entry and exit rules across historical trades.


### 1. Build the two-leg position


Open[AlgoTest Strategy Builder](https://algotest.in/strategy-builder) and select the underlying and expiry. Use the short-straddle template or add a sell call and sell put manually.


Check that both legs have the same strike, expiry and quantity. Review the premiums and payoff before proceeding. Accidentally selecting different expiries or unequal quantities changes the position being analysed.


### 2. Define a time-based strategy


In AlgoTest's 920 time-based workflow, select the underlying and configure your entry and exit times. Add two short option legs, one CE and one PE, with ATM strike selection and matching quantities and expiry settings.


For the detailed setup, follow the[9:20 straddle strategy walkthrough](https://algotest.in/blog/the-920-straddle-strategy-defined/) . Its entry time is an example to investigate, not a universally optimal time to trade.


### 3. Specify what happens when a trade goes wrong


Decide your leg-level and overall strategy stop-loss rules, time-based exits and any re-entry conditions before comparing results. AlgoTest's[overall strategy settings](https://docs.algotest.in/Time-Based-Algo-Trading/How-to-Master-Backtesting-on-AlgoTest/features/overall-strategy-settings/) explain the combined-position controls.


Consider what happens if one leg exits first. The remaining short option still carries directional risk. Re-entry also creates additional exposure and trading costs; it should be an explicit part of the tested rules.


### 4. Evaluate more than total profit


Use a review checklist:


-


**Drawdown:** how large were the losses from a previous equity peak?


-


**Losing streaks:** could the planned capital withstand consecutive losses?


-


**Trade distribution:** did a small number of days account for most of the result?


-


**Costs:** does the result remain useful after realistic fees and slippage?


-


**Stability:** does performance depend on one unusually favourable period or precise parameter choice?


Reserve a separate period to evaluate the rules after developing them. Repeatedly tuning settings to the same history can make the result look more dependable than it is.


### 5. Forward-test the chosen rules


Observe how the strategy behaves on incoming market data before committing capital. Compare intended entries, exits and risk controls with what actually occurs.


Historical prices and simulated fills cannot reproduce every live execution condition. Read AlgoTest's explanation of[why backtest, forward-test and live results differ](https://algotest.in/blog/why-is-there-is-difference-between-my-live-trade-vs-forward-test-vs-backtest-results/) when interpreting those differences.


## Short straddle risks and margin requirements


The call side has theoretically unlimited loss as the underlying rises. On the put side, loss is substantial but finite because the underlying cannot fall below zero. Both can greatly exceed the premium received.


Margin is collateral required to maintain the position, not its maximum possible loss. Requirements vary with the contract, market conditions, portfolio offsets and broker rules. Check the current requirement for the exact position and allow for adverse price movements.


A stop-loss is an exit instruction, not a guaranteed execution price. Gaps, fast price changes or insufficient liquidity can lead to a worse exit than planned. Monitor rejected orders and incomplete exits as well as the P&L.


Buying protective out-of-the-money options changes the structure. With appropriate wings, the position becomes an iron butterfly with defined expiry risk. Those options cost premium, so the resulting payoff must be evaluated separately.

All three use a common expiry for their two legs. A short strangle does not remove the open-ended upside risk of selling an unhedged call. For the long straddle, the maximum loss is the premium paid, plus costs.
